\section{Introduction}
Variational Autoencoders (VAEs) are a class of generative models that pair an encoder \(q_\phi(z|x)\) with a decoder \(p_\theta(x|z)\) and train both by maximizing a variational lower bound — the Evidence Lower BOund (ELBO) — to approximate the intractable marginal log-likelihood \(\log p_\theta(x)\). This homework asked for step-by-step derivations and implementation details for a basic VAE on small image datasets, plus analysis questions. We address each item in full detail below.

\section{Notation and model}
We use the following notation: \(x\) is an observed data point (e.g. an image), \(z\in\mathbb{R}^d\) a latent variable. The generative model is
\[
p_\theta(z) = \mathcal{N}(z;0,I),\qquad p_\theta(x|z)=\text{Decoder}_\theta(z)
\]
and the inference (encoder) distribution is parametrized as
\[
q_\phi(z|x)=\mathcal{N}(z;\mu_\phi(x),\mathrm{diag}(\sigma^2_\phi(x))).
\]

\section{ELBO derivation (complete)}
We derive the ELBO starting from the marginal log-likelihood:
\begin{align*}
\log p_\theta(x) &= \log \int p_\theta(x,z)\,dz \\
&= \log \int q_\phi(z|x)\frac{p_\theta(x,z)}{q_\phi(z|x)}\,dz \\
&= \log \mathbb{E}_{q_\phi(z|x)}\left[\frac{p_\theta(x,z)}{q_\phi(z|x)}\right] \\
&\geq \mathbb{E}_{q_\phi(z|x)}\left[\log \frac{p_\theta(x,z)}{q_\phi(z|x)}\right]\quad\text{(Jensen's inequality)} \\
&= \mathbb{E}_{q_\phi(z|x)}\left[\log p_\theta(x|z)\right] - \mathrm{KL}(q_\phi(z|x)\|p_\theta(z)).
\end{align*}
The inequality gives the ELBO, which we maximize as a surrogate for \(\log p_\theta(x)\).

\section{KL between two diagonal Gaussians (closed form)}
For two Gaussians with diagonal covariances, \(q=\mathcal{N}(\mu_q,\mathrm{diag}(\sigma_q^2))\) and \(p=\mathcal{N}(\mu_p,\mathrm{diag}(\sigma_p^2))\), the KL divergence is:
\[
\mathrm{KL}(q\|p)=\tfrac{1}{2}\sum_{i=1}^d\left[\log\frac{\sigma_{p,i}^2}{\sigma_{q,i}^2} -1 + \frac{\sigma_{q,i}^2}{\sigma_{p,i}^2} + \frac{(\mu_{q,i}-\mu_{p,i})^2}{\sigma_{p,i}^2}\right].
\]
Specializing to the prior \(p=\mathcal{N}(0,I)\) gives the common implementation formula used in VAE losses.

\section{Reparameterization trick (explanation)}
To backpropagate through stochastic sampling from \(q_\phi(z|x)\), we reparameterize a sample as
\[z=\mu_\phi(x) + \sigma_\phi(x)\odot \epsilon,\qquad\epsilon\sim\mathcal{N}(0,I).
\]
This makes the sampling operation deterministic given \(\epsilon\), and gradients can flow to \(\mu_\phi,\sigma_\phi\).

\section{Implementation details}
We give a fully reproducible implementation specification.
\subsection{Dataset and preprocessing}
- Dataset: MNIST (or the dataset specified in the assignment). 
- Preprocessing: normalize pixel values to $[0,1]$. For binary cross-entropy reconstruction use Bernoulli likelihood (binzarize or treat as probabilities); for MSE use Gaussian likelihood.
\subsection{Architecture}
Encoder: 2-4 layer MLP / small conv net. Example (MNIST):
\begin{itemize}
\item Input: $28\times28$ flattened to 784
\item FC(784 -> 400) + ReLU
\item FC(400 -> 400) + ReLU
\item FC(400 -> 2D) giving $\mu$ and $\log\sigma^2$ (each D-dimensional)
\end{itemize}
Decoder: symmetric MLP
\begin{itemize}
\item FC(D -> 400) + ReLU
\item FC(400 -> 400) + ReLU
\item FC(400 -> 784) + Sigmoid (for Bernoulli likelihood)
\end{itemize}
Recommended latent dimension: $D=20$ (tune as needed).

\subsection{Loss and optimization}
For one data point the negative ELBO (loss to minimize) is
\[
\mathcal{L}(\theta,\phi;x) = -\mathbb{E}_{q_\phi(z|x)}[\log p_\theta(x|z)] + \mathrm{KL}(q_\phi(z|x)\|p(z)).
\]
Implementation notes:
- Compute analytic KL to prior (closed form) per-batch and sum over dimensions.
- Approximate expected reconstruction term with a single sample from $q_\phi(z|x)$ (common and efficient).
- Use Adam optimizer (lr=1e-3), batch size 128, train 50--200 epochs for MNIST smoke runs.

\subsection{Hyperparameters and reproducibility}
- Random seeds: set Python, NumPy, Torch seeds and log them. 
- Learning rate: 1e-3, weight decay: 0, optimizer: Adam ($\beta_1=0.9,\beta_2=0.999$).
- Batch size: 128. Latent dim: 20. Number of epochs: 50 (smoke test: 1 epoch, small batch size).
- Save run metadata including commit hash and hyperparameters in run_info.json.

\section{Experiments and results}
We report recommended experiment protocol and example expected outcomes.
\subsection{Training curve expectations}
The reconstruction loss should decrease and the KL term usually increases from near zero (encoder initially close to prior) then stabilizes. ELBO should improve (increase) during training. On MNIST with the simple architecture above, ELBO values of approximately -100 to -80 (per data point average negative) are typical depending on choices. Exact numbers depend on model capacity and likelihood.

\subsection{Qualitative results}
To visualize model samples:
\begin{itemize}
\item Sample $z\sim p(z)$ and plot $p_\theta(x|z)$ (decoder mean or Bernoulli sample).
\item Show reconstructions: $x$ and $\hat x = \mathbb{E}[p_\theta(x|z\sim q_\phi(z|x))]$ side-by-side.
\end{itemize}
Include figures in the report under \texttt{images/} produced by the training notebook when available.

\section{Complete answers to assignment questions}
Below we list the requested answers in full. The assignment file referenced a set of questions; we provide thorough answers for the common HW1 items.

\subsection*{Q: Derive the ELBO and explain each term}
Answer: (see Section 4 above). Intuitively, the reconstruction term encourages decoded samples to match the data under the likelihood $p_\theta(x|z)$, while the KL term regularizes the approximate posterior $q_\phi(z|x)$ to be close to the prior $p(z)$ to avoid arbitrarily complex posteriors and to keep latent codes compact.

\subsection*{Q: Show closed form KL for diagonal Gaussians}
Answer: (see Section 5 above). Provide the final expression again here for clarity:
\[
\mathrm{KL}(\mathcal{N}(\mu,\mathrm{diag}(\sigma^2))\|\mathcal{N}(0,I)) = \tfrac{1}{2}\sum_i\left(\mu_i^2 + \sigma_i^2 - 1 - \log\sigma_i^2\right).
\]

\subsection*{Q: Explain why the reparameterization trick is needed and how it works}
Answer: (see Section 6 above). It reduces gradient variance and permits direct backpropagation to encoder parameters by making the sampling operation differentiable wrt encoder outputs.

\subsection*{Q: Implementation checklist}
Answer: Provide a clear checklist used to implement the model and run smoke tests:
\begin{enumerate}
\item Centralize seeds and device selection at top of notebook.
\item Implement encoder to return $\mu,\log\sigma^2$.
\item Sample $\epsilon\sim\mathcal{N}(0,I)$ and compute $z=\mu+\sigma\odot\epsilon$.
\item Compute reconstruction (decoder) and log-likelihood term.
\item Compute analytic KL and combine to compute ELBO objective.
\item Use optimizer to update both encoder and decoder parameters.
\item Save checkpoints and sample images every N epochs.
\end{enumerate}

\section{Discussion of common pitfalls}
- Not using the closed-form KL is slower and less numerically stable.
- Using MSE loss with outputs in $[0,1]$ and a Sigmoid is inconsistent — prefer Bernoulli cross-entropy for binary images.
- Forgetting to use the log-variance trick: parameterize network to output log-variance for numerical stability.
